# moments.py
*`src/pySEA/rayTEM/moments.py`*

Beam-envelope state and moment-closure models for rayTEM.

---

## Module-level functions

### `center_monomials(monomials, mu)` *(line 224)*
Rewrite an absolute-coordinate polynomial in deviations from the mean.

Absolute → central coordinates by binomial expansion, `2^n` terms for degree
`n` (8 for the cubic spherical kick). A no-op for a centered beam, so it costs
nothing in the common case; it matters when an element sits on a beam that has
already been displaced. **`_chromatic_monomials` must NOT go through this** —
its energy factor is a deviation by definition and would be wrongly re-expanded
about `μ_E`.

### `kick_moments(monomials_by_column, Sigma, closure)` *(line 293)*
Mean, cross-covariance and self-covariance of a polynomial kick.

The only place a closure assumption is applied. Returns `(delta_mean, C, D)`
with `C[a,c] = Cov(s_a, δ_c)` (asymmetric on purpose — the call site
symmetrizes with `M_l @ C + C.T @ M_l.T`; do not "fix" it) and
`D = Cov(δ, δ)` formed as `<δδ> − <δ><δ>`, which is what makes an even-order
aberration's mean shift come out as a shift rather than as extra width.
Loops over *all* column pairs, so cross-plane terms are included.
No aberration-specific algebra lives here: adding a nonlinear term means
emitting its monomials, not deriving its moments.

### `MomentClosure.moment(self, Sigma, indices)` *(line 93)*
The central moment :math:`\langle \prod_a s_{i_a} \rangle`.

The seam the plan asked for: beam state (`CovarianceBeam`) separated from the
assumption used to extend it. Deliberately **one** general method rather than a
menu of named cases, so swapping a closure changes physics rather than
relabelling it. A closure holding explicit third/fourth-moment tensors would
override `moment` for the degrees it holds and fall back for the rest.

**Consistency is the caller's responsibility.** The interface imposes none, and
a closure whose returned moments are not the moment set of any real
distribution will drive `Σ'` indefinite. `CovarianceBeam.is_positive_semidefinite`
is the guard.

<!-- AI: add class-level notes and cross-links below -->

### `GaussianMomentClosure.moment(self, Sigma, indices)` *(line 187)*
The central moment for ``indices`` by Wick pairing.

Recursive Wick pairing: pair the first index with each of the others, recurse
on the remainder. `(n−1)!!` pairings at degree `n` — 15 at degree six, the
highest a shipped aberration needs — so cost is negligible next to transport.

Because it evaluates the **exact** moments of `N(mu, Sigma)`, the resulting
`Σ'` is the exact pushforward of a Gaussian and therefore positive
semidefinite for *any* aberration strength. Large aberrations are an accuracy
problem, never a PSD problem. Truncating the closure is what breaks PSD.

Using it does not make the beam Gaussian. It is exact for one aberrated element
on a Gaussian beam and becomes an approximation only at a *second* nonlinear
element. That error is bounded by the excess kurtosis the first one induced,
`γ₂ = 27 f²` with `f` the aberration's share of the angular variance — so there
is no regime where the aberration matters to Σ but its non-Gaussianity does
not.

### `CovarianceBeam.__init__(self, mean, covariance, moment_closure, wavelength)` *(line 456)*
Store the state, the closure it was produced under, and the wavelength.

A **view** over the drivers' existing `.mu`/`.covariance_matrix`, not a second
store — reached as `section.covariance_beam` / `scope.covariance_beam`. Carries
the closure alongside the state so a result never loses track of the assumption
that produced it.

Prefer `emittance` to `sigma` when judging aberration damage: a width says
nothing on its own (a beam is wide at the detector because it was focused at
the specimen), while emittance is invariant under ideal transport and grows
only where something nonlinear acted. On `basic_column` an objective aberration
can be a `1e-4` share of the angular *variance* and still multiply the
*emittance* by ten, because emittance is a determinant and so responds to the
part of the kick uncorrelated with position — exactly the part no downstream
lens can undo.

### `CovarianceBeam.z(self)` *(line 547)*
Plane positions along the column.

### `CovarianceBeam.sigma(self, name)` *(line 565)*
RMS width of one column, per plane.

### `CovarianceBeam.correlation(self, a, b)` *(line 596)*
One covariance entry, per plane.

Signed, and the sign is the physics: it says whether the beam is converging or
diverging at that plane. It is a covariance, not a squared quantity — writing
it `σ_{x,xt}²` would be wrong.

### `CovarianceBeam.emittance(self, axis)` *(line 627)*
Transverse rms emittance, per plane.

`sqrt(σ_x²σ_xt² − σ_{x,xt}²)`, the phase-space area. Invariant under any ideal
linear transport (the sharpest available check that a column is behaving) and
raised by any nonlinear one (the sharpest available signal that an aberration
did something irreversible). Since each nonlinear element adds its own area,
`ε²` growth is very nearly a budget that sums, and the amount by which it fails
to sum is the inter-element coupling.

### `CovarianceBeam.real_space_ellipse(self, index)` *(line 719)*
Principal rms widths and axes of the real-space block.

### `CovarianceBeam.angular_ellipse(self, index)` *(line 761)*
Principal rms widths and axes of the angular block.

### `CovarianceBeam.momentum_covariance(self, index)` *(line 792)*
The angular block scaled to transverse momentum.

`k₀²Σ_uu` — purely a change of units, so the eigenvectors are those of
`angular_ellipse` and only the eigenvalues scale. Raises when no wavelength is
known rather than silently returning angles; `k₀` comes from
`Source(voltage=...)`.

### `CovarianceBeam.is_positive_semidefinite(self, tol)` *(line 839)*
Whether every plane's covariance is a physically possible one.

Cannot fail for the shipped `GaussianMomentClosure` (see above — the update is
an exact pushforward). It exists as a guard on **custom** closures and on any
future partial one, both of which can produce an unphysical `Σ'`. The tolerance
is relative because the transverse and energy columns differ by many orders of
magnitude and an absolute floor would be meaningless for one of them.

### `CovarianceBeam.at(self, index)` *(line 879)*
